rationale: Both accounts describe Sennacherib's invasion of Judah's fortified cities; Kings supplies the regnal year.
The Assyrian force advances specifically against Jerusalem, explaining the threat Hezekiah recognized.
The same chapter later identifies Hezekiah's blocking and redirection of Gihon's water, clarifying the water-defense consultation.
The same chapter supplies the named water outlet and its diversion into David's city behind the earlier denial of water to Assyria.
Both describe Jerusalem's walls and water defenses under military pressure; Isaiah adds a rebuke of reliance on those works, without identifying every construction as identical.
The law prescribes encouragement before battle grounded in God's saving presence, the substance of Hezekiah's address in the following verses; the speakers' offices differ.
Hezekiah's assurance that more are with Judah echoes Elisha's assurance that unseen divine defenders outnumber the enemy.
The command not to fear a larger enemy rests in both passages on the Lord's presence with His people in battle.
Hezekiah's claim that God will save and fight their war closely expresses the law's assurance that God fights with Israel to save it.
Both locate the Assyrian king's dispatch of envoys to Jerusalem at Lachish.
The Assyrian challenge in both accounts asks what basis Hezekiah has for his confidence.
Both speeches accuse Hezekiah of misleading Jerusalem by promising the Lord's rescue and urge rejection of his assurance.
Both Assyrian speeches misrepresent Hezekiah's removal of high places and restriction to one altar as grounds for distrusting divine help.
The Assyrian argument appeals to earlier conquests and the inability of the conquered nations' gods to rescue them.
Both speeches challenge Jerusalem to name a national god that rescued its land from Assyria and extend the challenge to the Lord.
The repeated demand not to believe Hezekiah culminates in the same claim that no god can deliver from Assyria.
Kings explicitly characterizes the Assyrian servants' words as reproach and blasphemy against the living God.
Kings preserves the threatening message and Hezekiah's reception of its letters, expanding the written reproach summarized here.
Both emphasize the loud Judean-language address audible to the people on Jerusalem's wall.
Hezekiah's prayer answers the Assyrian comparison by distinguishing the living God from conquered idols made by human hands.
Kings expands Hezekiah's prayer over the Assyrian letters and Isaiah's message that God heard it.
Both recount the angel's destruction of the Assyrian camp, the king's return, and his killing by his sons in his god's house.
The promised shielding of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Assyrian army provide the fuller parallel to this summary of deliverance.
Kings expands the same sequence of mortal illness, Hezekiah's prayer, divine healing, and a confirming sign.
The warning that prosperity can lift up the heart and produce forgetfulness of God illuminates Hezekiah's failure to respond to divine benefit.
Kings preserves Hezekiah's plea for peace in his days after the threat of Babylonian loss; Chronicles explicitly states that wrath was deferred following his and Jerusalem's humbling.
Kings describes Hezekiah's treasury of silver, gold, spices, equipment, and other stores shown to Babylonian visitors.
Chronicles attributes the king's abundant possessions to God, matching the command to recognize God as the giver of wealth rather than crediting one's own power.
Kings likewise credits Hezekiah with a fountain and aqueduct that brought water into the city.
Kings expands the visit of Babylonian envoys and Hezekiah's display of his treasures; Chronicles interprets the occasion as a test of his heart.
Both expressly describe divine testing as revealing what is in a person's heart.
Both closing notices refer readers to royal records for Hezekiah's remaining deeds; Chronicles additionally names Isaiah's prophecy.
Both close Hezekiah's reign with his death and burial and Manasseh's succession, while Chronicles adds the public honors.
Both give Manasseh's accession at twelve and fifty-five-year reign in Jerusalem.
Both judge Manasseh's conduct by the abominations of the nations displaced before Israel.
Both recount rebuilding Hezekiah's demolished high places, Baal worship, sacred groves, and worship of heaven's army.
Both contrast Manasseh's illicit altar-building in the temple with God's declaration that His name belongs in Jerusalem.
Both locate altars to heaven's army in the temple's two courts.
Both recount the king's children passing through fire and his use of divination and spirit practitioners as provocations against God.
The law specifically forbids the child-fire rites, omens, augury, sorcery, and spirit consultation gathered in Manasseh's offense list.
Both place an illicit carved image in the house God chose for His name, preserving the conflict between temple vocation and idolatry.
Both connect secure possession of the ancestral land with obedience to the commands given through Moses.
Both say Manasseh led the people into evil exceeding that of the nations removed before Israel.
Kings supplies the prophetic judgment against Manasseh and Judah that Chronicles summarizes as ignored divine speech.
Manasseh's captivity after idolatry illustrates the covenant warning of removal from the land and scattering among the nations; the law does not name his captors.
Seeking God in affliction after removal from the land follows the law's promise that distressed exiles may seek and return to the merciful Lord.
God's hearing and restoration of the humbled captive exemplify the promised divine mercy toward those who seek Him from exile.
Within the same chapter, Manasseh removes the foreign cult and temple images that the earlier verses identify as his own offenses.
Within the same chapter, Manasseh's order to serve Israel's God reverses his earlier service to heaven's army.
The people's continuing use of high places, though directed to the Lord, contrasts with the command to bring worship to His chosen place.
The same chapter's narrated prayer and answer supply the particular event recalled in the closing record notice; no lost source is identified with an extant text.
The same chapter has already narrated the high places, groves, and images catalogued in this retrospective record notice.
The closing notice's prayer and divine response refer back within the same chapter to Manasseh's humbling and restoration.
Both give Manasseh's death, burial in his house's garden, and Amon's succession.
Both give Amon's accession at twenty-two and two-year reign in Jerusalem.
Both portray Amon continuing his father's evil by serving the idols his father had served.
The same chapter supplies Manasseh's humbling and answered prayer, the explicit contrast to Amon's refusal to humble himself.
Both recount Amon's servants conspiring against him and killing him in his house.
Both recount the people's execution of Amon's conspirators and installation of Josiah.
Both give Josiah's accession at eight and thirty-one-year reign in Jerusalem.
Both assess Josiah as walking in David's ways without turning right or left.
Kings supplies corresponding purges of Baal worship and sacred groves; Chronicles alone supplies the youthful starting dates in this comparison.
Both describe reducing an illicit cult object to dust and scattering it over graves.
Josiah's destruction of altars, sacred groves, and images carries out the law's explicit commands against pagan worship sites.
The oracle specifically names Josiah and the burning of human bones upon an illicit altar, anticipating this action; Kings gives its Bethel setting.
Kings recounts Josiah's removal of high places and burning of human bones on their altars.
Both extend Josiah's purge beyond Judah into the northern cities; Kings speaks collectively of Samaria's cities rather than listing these tribes.
Both conclude the northern high-place purge with Josiah's return to Jerusalem.
Both place the commission to repair the Lord's house in Josiah's eighteenth year, with the scribe sent to arrange the work.
Both describe collected temple silver administered through the high priest and the entrance guards.
Both hand the temple funds to appointed workers for repairing the house.
Both specify builders, timber, and stone purchased for repairing the temple.
Both emphasize the repair workers' faithfulness; Kings connects that trustworthiness to the absence of demanded financial accounts.
David's assignment of Levites to scribal and judicial work supplies an institutional precedent for those Levite offices here, without equating the personnel.
Both recount the high priest's discovery of the book of law in the temple.
The law describes Moses writing the law book and entrusting it to the priests, providing context for a Mosaic law book discovered in the temple.
Both recount the priest announcing the discovery and giving the law book to the royal scribe.
Both combine the scribe's delivery to the king with his report that the temple funds reached the appointed workers.
Both reports state that the silver found in the temple was melted down and handed to the workers.
Both have the scribe tell the king that the priest supplied a book and then read it before him.
Both describe Josiah tearing his garments after hearing the law book's words.
Both list the priest, scribe, and royal representatives commissioned for the inquiry; the source calls one delegate Abdon while Kings calls him Achobor, without harmonizing the names.
Both commissions seek the Lord because the discovered book exposes ancestral disobedience and great divine anger.
Both place the royal inquiry before the prophetess married to Sellem in Jerusalem's masena/Masana; the accounts' differing ancestral names and robe-keeper wording are preserved.
Both introduce the prophetess's answer as the Lord God's message to the man who sent the delegation.
Both announce that the disasters written in the book read by the king will fall on this place.
Both give abandonment of God and incense to foreign gods as the cause of unquenchable wrath.
Both turn from judgment on the place to a distinct answer for the king who sought the Lord.
Both promise a hearing because Josiah humbled himself, tore his garments, and wept at the announced judgment.
Both promise that Josiah will be gathered to his grave before he sees the announced disasters on the place; neither comparison removes the later violent death account.
Both recount Josiah gathering the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.
Both recount public reading of the covenant book in the temple before the assembled people, great and small.

The public covenant reading follows the law's principle that assembled Israel hear and learn its words; the law's context specifies the Feast of Tents, whereas Chronicles describes Josiah's covenant assembly.
Both have the king stand by the pillar and covenant to obey the book with his whole heart and soul.
Kings explicitly says all the people stood in the covenant, corresponding to the assembly's participation required by Josiah.
Kings similarly summarizes Josiah's removal of abominations and wholehearted return to the Mosaic law.
Josiah's Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month follows the date prescribed for slaughter in Exodus.
Kings records Josiah's commanded Passover and places it in the same eighteenth regnal year supplied later in Chronicles.
David's division of priests by ancestral houses and ministerial service provides the organizational background for Josiah's priestly watches.
David's settlement of worship in Jerusalem ends the Levites' carrying work and turns them to temple ministry, closely matching Josiah's instruction here.
David's recorded arrangement of Levites by ancestral houses supplies the specific institutional background for the Levite preparation Josiah orders by David's writing.
The Levites' arrangement by ancestral houses for temple work explains the household divisions Josiah orders for festival service.
Josiah explicitly commands Passover slaughter according to Moses, whose law specifies the household animals and their slaughter.
The king's provision of lambs and young goats matches the permitted kinds of Passover animals; the additional calves belong to the wider festival provision.
Within the same chapter, the officials' contribution for priests supplements the king's large provision for the people, showing how the Passover animals were supplied.
Within the same chapter, the Levite leaders' provision complements the preceding contribution for priests, distinguishing the recipients rather than conflating the donors.
The priests' stations and divisions implement the earlier Davidic organization of ancestral houses for ministry.
Hezekiah's Passover likewise assigns slaughter to Levites and blood handling to priests, supplying a specific earlier example of the cooperation in Josiah's Passover.
The burnt offerings prepared for presentation are illuminated by the Mosaic instructions for dividing and placing the offering on the altar.
The Passover is roasted with fire exactly as Exodus requires; Chronicles separately distinguishes the other sacred portions boiled in vessels.
The Levites' preparation for Aaron's sons fulfills their established responsibility to assist priestly ministry and festival offerings.
David's appointment of the singing families of Asaph, Heman/Aiman, and Jeduthun/Idithon supplies the institutional background explicitly invoked for these singers.
Both portray Josiah's command as directing the nation's Passover observance.
The seven-day Unleavened Bread celebration follows the duration prescribed alongside Passover in Exodus.
Both describe Josiah's Passover as unparalleled among the monarchy's celebrations; Chronicles names Samuel while Kings refers to the judges.
Both date this Passover to Josiah's eighteenth regnal year.
This distinct suffixed source unit parallels the removal of spirit practitioners, teraphim, and idols to uphold the law book Hilkiah found; its stronger verb burned is preserved.
The law's prohibition of divination and spirit consultation explains the removal of those practices in this separate source unit.
This separate source unit closely parallels the unique assessment of Josiah's wholehearted return according to Moses' law.
Josiah's whole heart, soul, and strength correspond to the threefold commitment required in the command to love the Lord.
Both retain divine wrath against Judah because of Manasseh's provocations despite Josiah's reform.
Both announce Judah's removal like Israel and rejection of Jerusalem and the house bearing God's name.
Both describe Pharaoh's advance toward the Assyrian king at the Euphrates and Josiah's decision to meet him.
The same chapter explicitly interprets Neco's warning as words through God's mouth, explaining why refusal to heed it matters in Josiah's encounter.
Kings places Josiah's fatal encounter with Pharaoh at Mageddo, corresponding to the plain of Magedon here; Chronicles adds the ignored warning.
Within the same chapter, Josiah's arrow wound and request for removal lead directly to his transfer into a second chariot and death.
Both recount the servants' transport of Josiah to Jerusalem and his burial; Kings says he was transported dead, while Chronicles narrates transport before reporting death.
The same chapter's national mourning at Josiah's death supplies the occasion for the enduring lamentation described here; no extant lament is identified as Jeremiah's composition.
Both close Josiah's account with an appeal to royal records for the rest of his deeds.
Both recount the people anointing Josiah's son and installing him after Josiah's death.
Both give the successor's accession age of twenty-three and three-month reign in Jerusalem.
This separate suffixed unit supplies the same maternal name and parentage, Amital daughter of Jeremiah; the place forms Lobena and Lemna are preserved.
This separate source unit gives the same judgment of evil conduct according to the royal ancestors.
Both locate Pharaoh's removal of the king at Deblatha in Emath; Chronicles expressly says he bound him.
Both describe Pharaoh's imposed tribute and the king's removal to Egypt; Chronicles has one talent of gold while Kings has one hundred, and the amounts are not harmonized.
Both describe Pharaoh installing Eliakim, renaming him, and taking the displaced brother to Egypt where he died.
This separate source unit parallels the taxation of the land according to each person's assessment to pay Pharaoh's silver and gold.
Both give accession at twenty-five, an eleven-year reign, and evil conduct; their conflicting maternal names and parentage remain unharmonized.
Both describe the king serving Babylon's king for three years and then rebelling.
Both list Chaldean, Syrian, Moabite, and Ammonite raiders in fulfillment of prophetic speech; Chronicles additionally mentions Samaria and describes withdrawal.
Both attribute Judah's removal from God's presence to divine anger over Manasseh's sins.
The oracle expressly names Jehoiakim and condemns the shedding of innocent blood, illuminating the accusation here without harmonizing the differing statements about judgment.
Both describe Nebuchadnezzar gaining power over Judah's king; Chronicles specifies the king's fetters and removal to Babylon, while Daniel also emphasizes the captured temple vessels.
Both recount a portion of the temple vessels carried to Babylon and deposited in the conqueror's temple.
Both refer to the royal annals for Jehoiakim's remaining deeds; the comparison is limited to that record notice.

Jeremiah names Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim and announces his removal into Chaldean hands, supplying the prophetic judgment background to this brief condemned reign; the age and reign length are supplied by Chronicles.

Jeremiah's deportation-letter setting names Jeconiah among those already removed and Zedekiah as the ruling king who sends to Babylon, corroborating the succession setting without importing disputed kinship from Kings.
Both give Zedekiah's accession at twenty-one and eleven-year reign in Jerusalem.
Both judge Zedekiah's reign as evil before the Lord; Chronicles adds his refusal to humble himself before Jeremiah.
Ezekiel condemns the Jerusalem ruler's broken covenant and oath to Babylon's king as an offense against God's own oath, clarifying the religious gravity of this rebellion.
Kings likewise reports Zedekiah's breach with Babylon's king in the setting of divine anger against Jerusalem and Judah.
Jeremiah condemns Judah for placing abominations in the house bearing God's name, matching the temple defilement summarized here.
Both stress God's repeated early sending of prophets and the people's refusal to hear them.
Jeremiah likewise connects refusal to hear repeatedly sent prophets with the announced northern invasion and ruin.
Kings details the capture and severe treatment of Zedekiah, one component of the Chaldean devastation summarized here.
Kings itemizes the temple metalwork and utensils taken to Babylon, expanding this summary of plunder.
Kings recounts the burning of the Lord's house and Jerusalem's houses; the supplied target does not separately narrate the demolition of the wall.
Kings records the deportation of the remaining city population while noting poor people left to cultivate the land; it does not supply Chronicles' terminal kingdom reference.
The land keeping its neglected Sabbaths while desolate directly recalls the covenant sanction of exile and the land's Sabbath rest.
Jeremiah specifies seventy years of servitude and desolation, the duration Chronicles says was fulfilled; the land-Sabbath rationale comes from the law.
The promise to visit Babylon's exiles when seventy years are fulfilled and return them supplies the restoration expectation invoked in Cyrus's proclamation.
Ezra opens with the same first-year setting, fulfillment of Jeremiah's word, divine stirring of Cyrus, and written kingdom-wide proclamation.
Isaiah names Cyrus in connection with rebuilding Jerusalem and laying the foundation of God's house, matching Cyrus's stated commission here.
The oracle attributes Cyrus's victories and opened kingdoms to Israel's God for Israel's sake, illuminating Cyrus's acknowledgment of divinely given dominion.
Ezra preserves Cyrus's acknowledgment of the God of heaven, commission to build the Jerusalem temple, and invitation for God's people to go up, continuing the proclamation that closes Chronicles.
